name: Optionality
description: Originally a financial and strategic planning term used in Tier 4-5 corponation boardrooms to mean 'the value of keeping future choices open,' it leaked into common speech as a polite but cutting way to say someone is noncommittal, avoidant, or fundamentally unwilling to be accountable. 'He has a lot of optionality' means he will never commit to you, your cause, or your survival. The term carries particular venom in Tier 1-2 contexts where it describes people with enough resources to choose and who choose nothing.
cultural_impact: The word has become a standard piece of M88 vernacular across all tiers, though it means subtly different things depending on context — in Tier 5 it's still used neutrally; everywhere below Tier 3 it's almost always a quiet insult. The phrase 'optionality is a privilege' appears as graffiti throughout Shelf corridors.
key_figures: Praxis-7 (E.L.F. linguist documenting corporate-to-street language drift)
Counselor Fen Okafor-Brandt of Helixion Corp
story_hooks: A Tier 5 executive uses 'optionality' in its original neutral sense during a negotiation with a Tier 1 community leader — who hears it as a declaration of contempt — and the misread nearly collapses a fragile peace agreement.

Someone is writing a dictionary of corporate-to-street language drift and discovers that 'optionality' has developed a secondary meaning in Tier 1 specifically referring to people who survived by betraying others — a meaning no one in Tier 4 knows exists.
A synthetic being claims 'optionality' as a civil rights concept — arguing that synthetic beings are denied optionality by design — and the reframing goes viral across the BCI public net.
definition: Euphemism (originally corporate-neutral) for the state of having resources enough to avoid commitment. In street use: a polite but pointed accusation of cowardice, betrayal, or privilege-enabled non-accountability. 'He's got optionality' = he'll leave when it gets hard.
usage_example: 'Don't pitch your coalition idea to Brennan-Solis — that man has so much optionality he's practically vapor.'
spread: Fully spread across all tiers, but meaning has inverted as it descended — Tier 5 still uses it neutrally while Tier 1 uses it as a class-conscious insult.
